R.Br. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30033025-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=6 June 2021 |language=en}} }} [[File:Calystegia sepium MHNT.BOT.2009.7.11.jpg|thumb|''Calystegia sepium'' - [[MHNT]]]] '''''Calystegia sepium''''' or '''''Convolvulus sepium''''' ('''hedge bindweed''') is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Convolvulaceae]].{{cite web |title=Hedge Bindweed ''Calystegia sepium'' (L.) R.Br. |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.yeg |access-date=2026-08-20}} It has a [[cosmopolitan distribution|subcosmopolitan distribution]] throughout temperate regions of the North and South hemispheres. ==Description== ''Calystegia sepium'' is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plant that twines in a counter-clockwise direction to a height of up to {{convert|3|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}. The [[leaves]] are arranged alternately on the spiralling stem; they are dull green above and paler below, simple and sagittate (arrowhead shaped), {{convert|5–10|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3–7|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}} broad.{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}} The [[flower]]s are white, sometimes tinged pale pink, produced from late spring to the end of summer (between July and September in northern Europe).{{cite book |last1=Streeter |first1=David |last2=Hart-Davies |first2=Christina |title=Collins Flower Guide: the most complete guide to the flowers of Britain and Europe |publisher=HarperCollins |publication-place=London |date=2009 |isbn=978-0-00-718389-0 |page=368}}{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=251 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}} The buds are enclosed by large ({{convert|2|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}} long), ovate-lanceolate, green [[bracts|bracteoles]] with keels and burgundy margins; during [[anthesis]] they do not (or scarcely) overlap.{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=9780521707725}}{{rp|567}} The open flowers are trumpet-shaped, {{convert|3–7|cm|frac=4}} diameter. After flowering, the [[fruit]] develops as an almost spherical capsule, which is hidden by the bracts. It is {{convert|1|cm|frac=4}} in diameter, containing two to four large, dark brown, or black [[seed]]s that are shaped like quartered oranges. The plant thrives in hedges, fields, borders, beside water, on roadsides and woodland edges. ==Identification== There are several species of ''Calystegia'' which occur in similar habitats and can be difficult to distinguish, especially when not in flower. ''C. sepium'', ''C. silvatica'' and ''C. pulchra'' are sometimes recorded as an aggregate, as "''C. sepium'' agg.", whenever identification is uncertain. The use of this term can sometimes create confusion about which taxon is being discussed.{{cite web |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |title=BSBI species accounts: ''Calystegia sepium'' |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220716171430/https://sppaccounts.bsbi.org/content/calystegia-sepium-1.html |access-date=8 February 2022}} The best way to separate ''Calystegia sepium'' from the other taxa is by the bracteoles, which subtend the flower and wholly or partially encompass the sepals. ''Calystegia sepium'' has two rather long, narrow bracteoles which do not touch each other, whereas both large bindweed (''[[Calystegia silvatica]]'') and hairy bindweed (''[[Calystegia × pulchra]]'') have shorter, wider bracteoles which overlap where they meet.{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |title=Plant Crib |date=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}} {{Image frame|width=424|content=[[File:Calystegia sepium bracteoles.jpg|200px]] [[File:Calystegia silvatica bracteoles.jpg|218px]]|caption=Bracteoles of ''Calystegia sepium'' (left) and ''C. silvatica'' (right)|align=center}} ==Taxonomy== In research published in 2025, the genus ''[[Calystegia]]'' was found to be nested within the earlier-named genus ''[[Convolvulus]]'' , and its species are now being merged into that genus; this species thus becomes ''Convolvulus sepium'' L.{{cite journal |last1=Nepomuceno |first1=Silmara |last2=Fay |first2=Michael F |last3=Simões |first3=Ana Rita Giraldes |last4=Buril |first4=Maria Teresa |title=Character reconstruction and re-circumscription of the genus ''Convolvulus'' L. (Convolvulaceae) |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=209 |issue=4 |date=2025-12-01 |issn=0024-4074 |doi=10.1093/botlinnean/boaf023 |pages=359–380 |url=https://academic.oup.com/botlinnean/article/209/4/359/8116718 |access-date=2026-08-20|url-access=subscription }}{{cite web |title=Plants of the World Online |website=Plants of the World Online |date=2023-07-15 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30074933-2 |access-date=2026-08-20}} Eight regional [[subspecies]] are accepted: *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''americanus''. North America. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''angulatus''. North America. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''appalachianum''. Eastern North America. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''erraticus''. North America. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''balticus''. Northern Europe. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''roseatus''. Western Europe, coasts. Flowers pink. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''sepium''. Europe, Asia. *''Convolvulus sepium'' subsp. ''spectabilis''. Siberia. Flowers often pinkish. ==Phytochemistry== ''Calystegia sepium'' is toxic, containing calystegine alkaloids. {{Cite journal |last=Scholl |first=Yvonne |last2=Höke |first2=Dirk |last3=Dräger |first3=Birgit |date=December 2001 |title=Calystegines in ''Calystegia sepium'' derive from the tropane alkaloid pathway |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11669253_Calystegines_in_Calystegia_sepium_derive_from_the_tropane_alkaloid_pathway |journal=Phytochemistry |language=en |volume=58 |issue=6 |pages=883–889 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(01)00362-4}} ==Vernacular names== Apart from hedge bindweed, other vernacular names include ''greater bindweed, bearbind, hedge convolvulus, hooded bindweed, old man's nightcap, wild morning glory'', ''bride's gown, wedlock'' (referring to the white gown-like flowers and the binding nature of the vine), ''white witches hat, belle of the ball'',{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AIrNBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA921|page=921|title=World Economic Plants: A Standard Reference, Second Edition|year=2013|isbn=9781466576810|last1=Wiersema|first1=John H.|last2=León|first2=Blanca}} ''devil's guts and hedgebell''.{{cite web |title=''Calystegia sepium'' (Appalachia False Bindweed, Bearbind, Bellbind, Bingham's False Bindweed, Bracted Bindweed, Bugle Vine, Devil's Guts, Great Bindweed, Heavenly Trumpets, Hedgebell, Hedge False Bindweed, Large Bindweed (but cf. ''C. silvatica''), Old Man's Nightcap, Rutland Beauty, Wild Morning Glory) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/calystegia-sepium/ |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu |access-date=6 June 2021}} ==Similar species== *''[[Calystegia silvatica]]'', giant bindweed, is sometimes treated as a subspecies of ''C. sepium'' *''[[Convolvulus arvensis]]'', field bindweed, is a similar vine with much smaller features.
